hook_text: Look up at the Sun's light on a summer day. That light is eight minutes old. The starlight you see tonight may be older than you.
clip_script: On a clear night in the Karoo, look up. The Moon is brilliant, but it makes no light of its own. It is a rock, bouncing sunlight back to you. The stars, though, are luminous: they make their own light. And all of that light travels in straight lines, which is why shadows have sharp edges and you cannot see round a corner. It also travels incredibly fast: three hundred thousand kilometres every second, fast enough to circle the Earth seven and a half times in one second. But space is huge. Moonlight takes just over a second to reach you. Sunlight takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds. So when sunlight warms your face, you are feeling the Sun as it was eight minutes ago. And some of the faint stars above Sutherland are showing you light that set off before you were born.
visual_style: A whiteboard night sky over the Karoo with the Moon and stars, then a ray diagram from Sun to Moon to eye, then a clock ticking eight minutes as a beam travels from the Sun.
pacing: Slow and spacious, building to a striking final thought.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and calculate how old sunlight is.
